newsitem.title: GERMANY: German prosecutors absolve banks as tycoon charged.
newsitem.headline: German prosecutors absolve banks as tycoon charged.

text.p: Prosecutors probing one of Germany's biggest corporate scandals said Monday they charged tycoon Juergen Schneider with fraud and found no evidence to back defence allegations that his banks were to blame.
Outlining charges against the disgraced entrepreneur, the Frankfurt prosecutors' office said Schneider duped banks into extending credit by overstating rent income and forging bills.

Schneider, whose property empire collapsed under $3.2 billion of debt in 1994, has been charged with credit fraud, serious fraud and contributing to the bankruptcy of his company. He faces up to 15 years in prison.

The bankruptcy charge alleges he syphoned off about $157 million from his company and transferred the money to a Swiss bank account shortly before he fled the country. The money was transferred back to Germany last year to help repay creditors but Schneider has sued, claiming the money was his.
Prosecutors said they had found no evidence of wrongdoing by banks, contrary to repeated claims by Schneider that his creditors sabotaged him.

"In the investigation so far we have found no indications that criminal acts were conducted in the banks," Frankfurt prosecutor Dieter Haike told a news conference. "But mistakes were made. There is no such thing as an infallible examination of creditworthiness."

The Schneider bankruptcy in 1994 sparked fears of a German real estate slump, left hundreds of small craftsmen fighting for their livelihoods and exposed Schneider's banks to public outrage at the apparent ease with which he obtained funding.

Deutsche Bank, which bore the brunt of public criticism for loose lending and lax supervision, later that year accepted the resignation of four executives as a result of the debacle. But it maintained they had not behaved dishonourably.

Deutsche, Schneider's largest creditor, made matters worse for itself when its chief executive Hilmar Kopper dismissed as "peanuts" the millions of marks Schneider owed to small tradesmen and builders.
Schneider is being held in a local Frankfurt prison. If the Frankfurt district court approves the charges, the case is expected to go to trial this summer at the earliest.

Schneider's wife Claudia, who has been conditionally freed from detention because of concern for her health, has been charged with a bankruptcy offence and two associates have been charged with helping Schneider.
Schneider's Munich law firm could not be reached for comment Monday. His lawyer Christoph Rueckel said on Sunday that Schneider was committed to fighting the allegations.

Schneider, a bricklayer who became one of Germany's most celebrated entrepreneurs, gained fame by refurbishing historic hotels and stylish shopping malls in the post-unification property boom. But his empire crumbled because his rental income was too low to repay his debts.
He and his wife vanished in April 1994, sparking a year-long manhunt that ended with their arrest in Miami. They returned voluntarily to Germany last February.
The alleged fraud cited in the charges involve statements he allegedly made to Deutsche Bank, Dresdner Bank AG, BHF-Bank AG, Norddeutsche Landesbank and Deutsche Bau- und Bodenbank AG.

In one case, in which Deutsche was allegedly defrauded of $28 million in 1992, Schneider was accused of having presented forged rental agreements to secure credit for the Zeilgalerie shopping mall in the centre of Frankfurt.
In another, Schneider allegedly caused $30 million worth of damage to Norddeutsche Landesbank by overstating the price he paid to buy property in central Berlin.
